digest.top_line: DASL-HiCaP: darolutamide added to 96wk ADT + pelvic nodal RT gives 4y MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66) at interim, very high-risk localised or post-RP prostate.
digest.tldr: Prostate carried the day: DASL-HiCaP adds a second ARSI-intensification signal on an RT backbone, though at interim with OS (HR 0.88) and PCSS immature. CNS was negative: trotabresib added to RT/TMZ in IDH-wt ndGBM gave mPFS 7.9 vs 8.2 mo, 12-mo PFS 22.2% vs 38.9%, with more dose modifications. A surgical BM series links post-RT progression to FOXP3+ enrichment.

sites.intro: Two RT-adjacent readouts: a randomized phase II that found no benefit from adding a BET inhibitor to RT/TMZ, and a resection series profiling brain metastases that progressed after cranial RT.

studies.name: Trotabresib + RT/TMZ in newly diagnosed IDH-wt GBM
studies.tldr: mPFS 7.9 vs 8.2 mo with trotabresib added to RT/TMZ; 12-mo PFS 22.2% vs 38.9% (p 0.048), favoring SOC alone in ndGBM.
details: 🔍 Randomized phase II, 2:1, N=184 (124 trotabresib + SOC vs 60 SOC alone)
🔍 Newly diagnosed IDH wild-type GBM; SOC = surgery, RT, temozolomide
💊 Trotabresib: oral BET inhibitor, brain-penetrant; 30 mg/day 4 days on/24 off was the dose established in prior SOC combination
📊 PFS did not favour the experimental arm at median f/u 15 mo (136 PFS events)

details.text: 📊 Efficacy, trotabresib + SOC (arm A) vs SOC (arm B)
⚠️ G3+ TRAEs, arm A vs arm B
⚠️ TRAE-driven dose modifications, arm A vs arm B

details: ⚠️ Authors suggest the dose modifications may have compromised SOC delivery; RT-specific interruptions or dose received not reported in source
⚠️ PFS by local investigator RANO, no central review stated; MGMT status not reported in source
⚠️ RT dose/fractionation not reported in source

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase II, primary PFS endpoint not met with a 12-mo PFS signal favoring control; reinforces RT/TMZ alone. Abstract only, local RANO assessment.
verdict.audience: Newly diagnosed IDH wild-type glioblastoma, post-surgery

studies.significance: The 12-mo PFS gap (22.2% vs 38.9%) runs against the add-on, alongside excess G3+ thrombocytopenia (37% vs 15.3%) and dose interruptions (OR 2.43). For RT planning, the open question is whether myelosuppression from a concurrent add-on erodes chemoRT delivery; RT completion was not reported in source.

primary_endpoint.name: Progression-free survival
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: Not met; 12-mo PFS 22.2% vs 38.9% (p 0.048), favoring SOC

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized phase II**, 2:1, N=184. Median follow-up 15 mo; 136 PFS events at database lock.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Newly diagnosed IDH wild-type GBM** receiving SOC of surgery, RT and temozolomide. MGMT status and extent of resection not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Trotabresib, an oral **BET inhibitor**, added to SOC (arm A, n=124) vs SOC alone (arm B, n=60). Prior work established 30 mg/day 4 days on/24 days off with SOC.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT is the shared SOC backbone in both arms. Dose, fractionation and RT completion were **not reported in source**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** PFS from randomization to RANO progression by local investigators or death. Secondary: OS; safety by CTCAE v5 with dose modifications compared by OR.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **PFS not improved**; 12-mo PFS favored the control arm, and OS was identical (p 0.898).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ thrombocytopenia **37% vs 15.3%**, neutropenia 16.8% vs 8.5%. Dose reductions **43.7% vs 18.6%** (OR 3.39) and interruptions 49.6% vs 28.8% (OR 2.43).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RT plus concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide (the EORTC/NCIC regimen) remains the reference. This trial joins a long list of add-ons to that backbone that failed to move PFS or OS in ndGBM.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents newly diagnosed IDH wild-type GBM on standard RT/TMZ. Does not represent recurrent GBM or IDH-mutant glioma.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Local rather than central RANO review is vulnerable to pseudoprogression misclassification early after chemoRT. The 2:1 allocation leaves only 60 control pts, so the 12-mo PFS gap carries wide uncertainty.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors attribute part of the harm signal to **compromised SOC delivery** from TRAE-driven dose changes. Whether TMZ or RT dose intensity actually fell is not shown in the abstract, so the mechanism remains a hypothesis.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest reading of this trial is that a biologically plausible, brain-penetrant epigenetic agent failed in exactly the way many add-ons to the RT plus temozolomide backbone have failed in newly diagnosed glioblastoma: no PFS gain, no OS gain, and added toxicity. What makes it more instructive than a simple null is the direction of the 12-month PFS landmark. A rate of 22.2% versus 38.9% with p 0.048 is not a neutral result. It suggests that, at least through the first year, adding trotabresib may have made things worse, even though medians (7.9 vs 8.2 months) and OS (16.9 vs 16.7 months) converged.

The authors' explanation is that overlapping myelosuppression forced dose reductions and interruptions (43.7% and 49.6% vs 18.6% and 28.8%), which may have compromised delivery of standard therapy. That is a reasonable hypothesis, and the G3+ thrombocytopenia rate of 37% versus 15.3% makes it biologically credible, since thrombocytopenia is also the toxicity that most often interrupts concurrent temozolomide. But the abstract does not show that SOC dose intensity fell. It reports modifications attributed to TRAEs without separating trotabresib reductions from temozolomide reductions or RT breaks. For a radiation oncologist, the missing piece is RT completion: whether pts in arm A finished their course on schedule. Without it, the claim that SOC delivery was compromised is inference, not observation.

Several design features should temper confidence in the PFS harm signal itself. Progression was assessed by local investigators using RANO, without stated central review. In the months after chemoRT, pseudoprogression is common in glioblastoma, and unblinded local reads in an add-on trial can shift early progression calls in either direction. The 2:1 allocation left 60 control pts, so the control-arm 12-month PFS estimate is fragile. MGMT promoter status, the dominant prognostic and predictive factor for temozolomide benefit, is not reported in the abstract, and an imbalance across arms of that size could plausibly produce a landmark gap of this magnitude on its own.

The OS result is the more trustworthy endpoint here, and it is flat. That makes the practical conclusion straightforward: RT plus temozolomide alone remains the reference for newly diagnosed IDH wild-type disease, and trotabresib at this schedule has no role in it. The broader lesson the authors draw, that a new agent in this setting must be tolerable enough not to erode delivery of the backbone, is worth taking seriously for trial design. Concurrent agents with hematologic toxicity overlapping temozolomide carry a real risk of trading backbone intensity for an unproven benefit. What the trial cannot settle is whether BET inhibition has any activity in glioblastoma at a dose and schedule that spares the marrow, or in an adjuvant-only window after chemoRT is complete.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Concurrent trotabresib added hematologic toxicity during chemoRT without PFS or OS gain, and the authors flag compromised SOC delivery as a possible driver. RT completion and interruption data were not reported in source, so whether the RT course itself was affected stays unknown.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: A brain-penetrant BET inhibitor added to TMZ gave mPFS 7.9 vs 8.2 mo and mOS 16.9 vs 16.7 mo, with dose reductions at OR 3.39. Overlapping myelosuppression with TMZ (G3+ thrombocytopenia 37% vs 15.3%) is the lesson for designing the next add-on in this setting.

open_questions: Was RT or temozolomide dose intensity actually reduced in the trotabresib arm?
Does MGMT status explain the 12-mo PFS gap?
Would adjuvant-only BET inhibition avoid overlapping chemoRT toxicity?

studies.name: Inflammatory and epigenetic signatures in progressive brain metastases after cranial RT
studies.tldr: BM progressing after cranial RT showed CD8+ TILs 44 vs 187 cells/mm2 and FOXP3+ 215 vs 41 vs treatment-naive BM, an immunosuppressive shift.
details: 🔍 ESMO 2026 abstract 703RO (rapid oral), N=153 pts resected for progressive BM
🔍 Exome sequencing, DNA methylation profiling and IHC on resected specimens

details.text: 📊 TIL densities, progression after prior RT vs treatment-naive BM (median cells/mm2)

details: 📊 Paired relapse subset: 35 treatment-naive pts had a second resection; 34.3% got CNS-RT in between
📊 Irradiated relapses showed modest hypermethylation in immunomodulation and therapy-resistance pathways
📊 No difference in mutational profile between progressive lesions, irrespective of prior therapy
⚠️ p-values, CIs and effect sizes for TIL differences not reported in source
⚠️ RT technique (SRS vs WBRT), dose, and RT-to-resection interval not reported
⚠️ Surgical cohort selects resectable progression; steroid exposure and primary histology not stated

verdict.rationale: Translational tissue cohort with no clinical endpoint; post-RT group n=43, RT technique and timing unreported, no statistics in source. Hypothesis-generating for IO sequencing only.
verdict.audience: Progressive brain metastases resected after prior cranial RT

studies.significance: The RT read is the paired relapse subset: within the same pts, irradiated relapses carried hypermethylation in immunomodulation pathways, while the cross-sectional comparison showed FOXP3+ 215 vs 41 cells/mm2. RT technique, dose and timing are absent, so this cannot yet inform whether SRS should precede or follow IO.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Tissue-based cohort of **153 pts** undergoing resection for progressive BM, presented as ESMO 2026 rapid oral **703RO**. Prospective vs retrospective design not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Stratified by prior treatment: **RT n=43**, systemic n=37, RT + systemic n=10, **treatment-naive n=63**. Primary histology not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Exposure described only as prior cranial / CNS radiotherapy. **Modality, dose, fractionation and interval to resection not reported.**

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Post-RT progressive BM showed lower immune-activating TILs and **higher FOXP3+ density** than treatment-naive BM (table). Methylation changes after RT were described as **modest**; no mutational differences.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The prevailing rationale for combining SRS with checkpoint inhibitors rests on RT priming antitumor immunity. This tissue signal points the other way in lesions that have already failed RT, without testing any combination.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents resectable BM progressing after prior cranial RT. Does not represent responding or radiographically stable irradiated lesions, or unresected progression.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Cross-sectional post-RT vs naive comparison mixes different pts and disease timepoints. Steroids, radionecrosis admixture and histology are uncontrolled; no p-values reported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support an immunosuppressed microenvironment in RT-refractory BM, consistent with variable IO responses post-RT. Whether RT causes the shift or selects for lesions that already had it is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
The central observation is that brain metastases coming to resection after failing cranial radiotherapy look immunologically cold and regulatory-skewed compared with untreated lesions: CD8+ density 44 vs 187 cells/mm2 and FOXP3+ 215 vs 41. For a radiation oncologist, that sits awkwardly against the dominant clinical narrative, in which focal RT is expected to release antigen, recruit effector cells and justify pairing SRS with checkpoint blockade. The two views are not necessarily in conflict. Immune priming is usually framed as an early effect in a responding lesion; this cohort samples only lesions that progressed, often at an unstated interval after RT. A lesion resected because it grew through radiation is, by construction, the subset in which any priming failed.

That selection problem is the main methodological reason to hold the result loosely. The post-RT and treatment-naive groups are different patients at different points in their disease, and the source does not report histology, systemic therapy exposure within the RT group, or steroid use, any of which could depress TIL counts independently of radiation. Corticosteroids in particular are routine around cranial RT and symptomatic progression and would push in the same direction as the observed finding. No p-values or intervals accompany the medians, so the size of the uncertainty around a 43-patient arm is unknown. Radiation necrosis admixed in the specimen could also alter density measurements per mm2.

The stronger design element is the paired relapse subset: 35 initially untreated patients resected twice, with 34.3% receiving CNS radiotherapy between operations. Within-patient comparison removes much of the confounding by histology and host. Here the authors describe only modest methylation changes, enriched for immunomodulation, therapy resistance and neurovascular interaction pathways, and they do not report whether TIL composition shifted in the same patients. That missing piece is the one that would distinguish RT inducing immunosuppression from RT selecting for already-suppressed clones. The absence of any mutational difference between groups argues against a simple genetic-selection story, but exome data are a coarse test of that.

What the abstract does not give is any RT parameter. Single-fraction SRS to a small target, fractionated SRS to a resection cavity, and whole-brain RT deliver very different lymphocyte exposure and very different tissue injury, and the immunologic consequences may not be the same. Until the full presentation separates technique and timing, this cannot inform whether IO should precede, accompany or follow cranial RT, or whether progression after RT should change the choice of salvage systemic therapy. What it does support is sampling RT-refractory lesions when resected and building that tissue question into sequencing trials, rather than assuming irradiated progression behaves like an untreated metastasis.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Irradiated relapses in the paired subset showed hypermethylation in immunomodulation pathways, and post-RT lesions carried FOXP3+ 215 vs 41 cells/mm2. Without SRS vs WBRT, dose or timing, it cannot yet steer RT sequencing around IO.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Progressive BM after cranial RT showed CD8+ 44 vs 187 cells/mm2 versus untreated lesions, a microenvironment that may explain variable IO responses post-RT. It raises, but does not answer, whether salvage systemic choice should differ after RT failure.

open_questions: Optimal sequencing of cranial RT and immunotherapy in BM
Does post-RT immunosuppression differ by SRS vs WBRT?
Does RT induce or select the immunosuppressed phenotype?

studies.name: DASL-HiCaP
studies.tldr: 4y MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66), adding darolutamide to 96wk ADT + pelvic nodal RT in very high-risk localised or post-RP persistent/recurrent prostate cancer.
details: 🔍 Phase 3, placebo-controlled, randomised 1:1, N=1,106 (553 per arm), randomised 30APR20 to 09AUG23
💊 Darolutamide 600 mg vs placebo BID for 96 wk, on a 96 wk LHRH analog backbone
🔍 RT to prostate/prostate bed and pelvic nodes in both arms, definitive or salvage
📐 Single prespecified interim after 87 MFS-CI events; disclosure boundary 2-sided stratified log-rank p<0.012

details.text: 📊 Efficacy at interim, median f/u 3.8y (events, event-free at 4y)

details: 📊 MFS benefit consistent across prespecified subgroups, incl primary vs salvage RT and with/without pelvic nodal involvement (OncLive); subgroup HRs not in source
⚠️ Interim read: trials stopped early on efficacy tend to overestimate effect size
⚠️ OS and PCSS immature; ICECaP surrogacy of MFS-CI for OS not yet confirmed in this trial
⚠️ Staging and MFS endpoint by CT/bone scan, not PSMA PET
⚠️ RT dose/fractionation not reported in source
🔗 vs STAMPEDE abiraterone in high-risk M0: a second ARSI-intensification signal with RT, different drug and backbone

verdict.rationale: Placebo-controlled phase 3 crossed its prespecified interim boundary, but interim-analysis gate holds until final analysis; OS and PCSS events too few to read.
verdict.audience: Very high-risk localised PC, or PSA persistent/recurrent ≤1y post-RP

studies.significance: RT was fixed in both arms (prostate or prostate bed plus pelvic nodes, 96 weeks of LHRH analog), so the 4y MFS-CI gain of 95% vs 88% is darolutamide layered on elective nodal RT. Benefit held across salvage-RT and node-involved subgroups per OncLive (subgroup HRs not in source); dose and fractionation not reported.
studies.monday_clinic: In very high-risk localised prostate cancer, or PSA persistence/recurrence within 1 year of RP, receiving 96 weeks of ADT with prostate and pelvic nodal RT, this supports discussing darolutamide intensification; it does not address shorter ADT, prostate-only fields, or PSMA-PET-staged disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International, **placebo-controlled, randomised 1:1 phase 3** (ANZUP1801), N=1,106. **Single prespecified interim** after 87 MFS-CI events, disclosure if 2-sided p<0.012. Median follow-up **3.8 years** (IQR 3.3 to 4.5).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Very high-risk localised** prostate cancer, or **biochemically persistent/recurrent disease within 1 year after RP**. Median age 71, pelvic nodal involvement on CT 29%, Gleason 9-10 in 73%, prior RP 15%.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: LHRH analog for **96 weeks** in all pts, plus **darolutamide 600 mg BID vs placebo for 96 weeks**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Definitive or salvage RT to **prostate/prostate bed and pelvic nodes** in both arms. Dose, fractionation and technique not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: MFS by conventional imaging** (CT and/or Tc bone scan), chosen per ICECaP surrogacy for OS. Secondary: PSA-PFS, PCSS, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G≥2 fatigue/asthenia **14% vs 10%**, hypertension 7% vs 9%, fractures 2% vs 3%, cardiac 3% vs 3%. **Any G≥3 AE 43% vs 36%**; no new safety signals per OncLive.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Joins STAMPEDE's abiraterone M0 data as evidence that ARSI intensification on top of ADT plus RT reduces metastasis in high-risk non-metastatic disease. Here the ARSI is darolutamide, placebo-controlled, with **mandated pelvic nodal RT** and a salvage cohort, which STAMPEDE did not test the same way.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents very high-risk localised or early post-RP persistent/recurrent prostate cancer staged by CT/bone scan, treated with 96 weeks of ADT and pelvic nodal RT. Does not represent PSMA-PET-staged pts, prostate-only RT fields, shorter ADT courses, or salvage beyond 1 year after RP.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Conventional imaging** for staging and the endpoint, so PSMA-era stage migration is unaccounted for. Prior RP only 15%, so the salvage subgroup is small despite a consistent direction. RT dose not reported, and the **G≥3 AE excess** sits against an OS signal that is still uninformative.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The MFS-CI and PSA-PFS reductions are large and concordant, but at 3.8 years of follow-up most deaths in both arms were not prostate cancer deaths, so the surrogate has to carry the case until OS matures. Whether 96 weeks of darolutamide is needed, or how this compares with other ARSIs in the same setting, is not settled.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest reading of DASL-HiCaP is as a systemic intensification trial run on a fixed, aggressive local backbone. Every pt received 96 weeks of an LHRH analog and RT covering the prostate or prostate bed plus the pelvic nodes, so the trial says nothing about whether RT fields or ADT duration matter. It says that, once those are maximised, adding darolutamide still roughly halves metastatic events by conventional imaging. For a radiation oncologist the useful framing is that the control arm already resembles aggressive contemporary practice for very high-risk disease, which makes the magnitude more credible than it would be against an older, thinner comparator.

The endpoint choice is deliberate. The investigators picked MFS by conventional imaging because ICECaP established it as a surrogate for OS in localised disease, and they kept CT and bone scan imaging consistent with that surrogate rather than switching to PSMA PET. That is methodologically defensible: a PSMA-defined endpoint would not carry the validated link to survival. The cost is transferability. A cohort staged by CT, with 29% pelvic nodal involvement visible on CT, is not the same population a PSMA-staged clinic sees, and some of these pts would have been upstaged elsewhere. The relative benefit may hold, but absolute numbers in a PSMA-selected group could look different.

The interim nature deserves weight beyond the verdict label. Trials that cross an efficacy boundary early tend to report effect estimates larger than the eventual truth, simply because the analysis happened at a moment of favourable random variation. With 27 versus 63 MFS events the confidence interval is wide, and the HR 0.42 point estimate is better treated as the optimistic end of the plausible range. The concordant PSA-PFS result (HR 0.47) supports the direction but shares the same follow-up window.

The survival data are honestly uninformative rather than negative. PCSS events were 4 versus 7 and OS events 21 versus 24, meaning most deaths in both arms came from causes other than prostate cancer at 3.8 years median follow-up. That is expected in a population with median age 71 and a high cure rate, and it is exactly why the surrogate was chosen. It also means that the excess in any G≥3 AE (43% vs 36%) is being weighed against a benefit that has not yet shown up in the outcome pts care about most. Fractures and cardiac events were balanced, which is reassuring for an older population.

Against STAMPEDE's abiraterone data in high-risk M0 disease, this is a second, independently designed, placebo-controlled signal that ARSI intensification with RT reduces metastasis. It adds a salvage cohort and mandated nodal RT, though with only 15% post-RP pts the salvage evidence rests mostly on a consistent subgroup direction reported by trade press without numbers. The decisions it leaves open are duration, whether a shorter darolutamide course would suffice, and whether pts on prostate-only fields or shorter ADT would benefit similarly. The result would be wrong in its practical implication if MFS-CI failed to translate into OS at final analysis, which is the question the ongoing follow-up is designed to answer.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: RT was fixed in both arms (prostate or prostate bed plus pelvic nodes, 96 weeks of LHRH analog), so the 4y MFS-CI gain of 95% vs 88% is darolutamide layered on elective nodal RT. Benefit held across salvage-RT and node-involved subgroups per OncLive; subgroup HRs and RT dose not in source.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Darolutamide 600 mg BID for 96 weeks on top of 96 weeks of LHRH analog cut MFS-CI events 27 vs 63 (HR 0.42), with PSA-PFS HR 0.47. The price is G≥3 AEs of 43% vs 36%, while fractures and cardiac events were similar; OS HR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.59) remains uninformative.

open_questions: Does the MFS-CI benefit translate into OS at final analysis?
Benefit in PSMA-PET-staged very high-risk pts?

papers.title: Darolutamide with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and definitive or salvage locoregional radiation therapy (RT) for localised, very high-risk prostate cancer: Interim analysis of an international, placebo-controlled, randomised phase 3 trial (DASL-HiCaP; ANZUP1801)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract LBA4 · Presidential Symposium I · 2026-10-24 · presented by Tamim Niazi (Montreal, Canada, QC) · NCT04136353

Background: We evaluated the addition of darolutamide to standard of care ADT and RT for very high-risk localised or biochemically persistent/recurrent prostate cancer within 1 year after radical prostatectomy (RP).
Methods: Participants (pts) were prescribed an LHRH analog for 96 weeks plus RT to prostate/prostate bed and pelvic nodes and randomised 1:1 to darolutamide 600 mg vs placebo, twice daily for 96 weeks. The primary endpoint was metastasis-free survival based on conventional imaging with CT and/or technetium bone scan (MFS-CI, as per ICECaP surrogacy for OS). PSA-progression free survival (PFS), prostate cancer specific survival (PCSS), and overall survival (OS) were secondary endpoints. The protocol specified a single interim analysis after 87 MFS-CI events, with IDSMC review for external disclosure if the 2-sided, stratified log-rank p-value for MFS-CI was <0.012.
Results: We randomised 1,106 pts from 30APR20 to 09AUG23 with median age 71 (IQR 65-75), pelvic nodal involvement on CT in 29%, Gleason score 9-10 in 73%, and prior RP in 15%. Median follow-up was 3.8 years (IQR 3.3 to 4.5). MFS-CI was longer amongst those assigned darolutamide vs placebo: 4-year MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, hazard ratio 0.42 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.66), 27 vs 63 events, p=0.0001. PSA-PFS, PCSS, and OS are shown below. The proportions of pts experiencing grade ≥2 of the following AE clusters of special interest (darolutamide vs placebo) were: fatigue/asthenia (14% vs 10%), hypertension (7% vs 9%), fractures (2% vs 3%), and cardiac (3% vs 3%). Any AE grade ≥3 was experienced by 43% vs 36% of pts, respectively.
Conclusions: Darolutamide significantly improved MFS-CI when added to ADT and loco-regional RT for very high-risk localised, or biochemically persistent/recurrent prostate cancer. Follow-up is ongoing to confirm the surrogacy of MFS-CI for OS. Table: LBA4 DarolutamideN=553 events (event-free at 4y) PlaceboN=553 events (event-free at 4y) Hazard ratio (95% CI) MFS 27 (95%) 63 (88%) 0.42 (0.27 to 0.66) PSA-PFS 46 (91%) 95 (83%) 0.47 (0.33 to 0.67) PCSS 4 (99%) 7 (99%) 0.58 (0.17 to 1.97) OS 21 (97%) 24 (95%) 0.88 (0.49 to 1.59)
Clinical trial identification: NCT04136353.

papers.title: Inflammatory and epigenetic signatures in progressive brain metastases after cranial radiotherapy
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 703RO · Rapid oral: CNS tumours · 2026-10-23 · presented by Ariane Steindl (Vienna, Austria)

Background: Given the high rate of early recurrence in brain metastases (BM), factors driving progression remain poorly understood. This study aimed to characterize genetic, epigenetic, and inflammatory signatures in progressive BM after different therapeutic strategies.
Methods: A total of 153 patients undergoing surgical resection for progressive BM were included and stratified according to prior treatment: radiotherapy (n=43), systemic therapy (n=37), radio- and systemic therapy (n=10), or treatment-naive (n=63). Tumor specimens were analyzed with exome-sequencing, DNA methylation profiling, and immunohistochemistry.
Results: Compared with treatment-naive BM, BM resected due to progression to prior radiotherapy demonstrated significantly reduced densities of immune-activating tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) such as CD3+ (median 71 vs. 494 cells/mm2,), CD8+ (44 vs. 187 cells/mm2), and CD45RO+ cells (104 vs. 302 cells/mm2). In contrast, densities of immunosuppressive TILs were increased (FOXP3+: 215 vs. 41cells/mm2). Among treatment-naive patients, 35 developed intracranial relapse and underwent a second resection. Of these, 65.7% did not receive any therapy in between, whereas 34.3% received CNS-radiotherapy between resections. Here, patients who received radiotherapy exhibited modest alterations in DNA methylation compared to those without radiotherapy. These changes were predominantly characterized by hypermethylation in irradiated lesions including pathways associated with immunomodulation, therapy resistance, and interactions with the neural and vascular microenvironment. Comparative genetic profiling did not identify differences in the mutational landscape between progressive lesions, irrespective of prior therapy.
Conclusions: In this study, BM progressing after prior cranial radiotherapy were associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, along with modest DNA methylation changes and enrichment of pathways related to immunomodulation and tumor survival. In combination with the clinical observation of varying responses to immunotherapy in progressive BM post-radiotherapy, our data warrant for further investigation for the optimal treatment sequencing in BM patients.

papers.title: Randomized phase II trial investigating addition of trotabresib (CC-90010) to radiotherapy and temozolomide in patients with newly diagnosed IDH wild-type glioblastoma
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 692O · Proffered paper: CNS tumours · 2026-10-25 · presented by Angelo Dipasquale (Rozzano, Italy) · NCT04324840

Background: Patients with IDH wild-type glioblastoma (GBM) invariably experience recurrence despite standard-of-care (SOC) including surgery, radiotherapy, and temozolomide. Bromodomain and extra-terminal proteins (BET) are epigenetic regulators of cell cycle progression overexpressed in GBM. Trotabresib (T) is an oral BET inhibitor that showed brain penetration and tolerable safety profile at a dose of 30 mg/day 4 days on/24 days off in combination with SOC.
Methods: Patients with newly diagnosed IDH wild-type GBM (ndGBM) were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive T + SOC (arm A) or SOC alone (arm B). The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time from randomization to RANO disease progression by local investigators or death. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from randomization to death. Safety profile was assessed with CTCAE V5 and dose reductions/interruptions between arms were compared using odds ratios (ORs).
Results: A total of 184 patients were randomized to arm A (n=124) or arm B (n=60). At the time of database lock, 136 patients experienced a PFS event. At a median follow-up of 15 months, PFS did not favour the experimental arm, with a median PFS (mPFS) of 7.9 vs 8.2 months and 12-month PFS rates of 22.2% vs 38.9% in arms A and B, respectively (p 0.048). No difference in OS was observed (median OS: 16.9 vs 16.7 months in arms A and B, respectively; p 0.898). The most frequent ≥ grade 3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and lymphopenia (37%, 16.8%, and 8.4% in arm A vs 15.3%, 8.5%, and 11.9% in arm B). Dose reductions and interruptions due to TRAEs were significantly more frequent in arm A (43.7% and 49.6%) than in arm B (18.6% and 28.8%), with ORs of 3.39 (95% CI 1.64–7.02; p 0.001) and 2.43 (95% CI 1.25–4.74; p 0.009), respectively.
Conclusions: The addition of trotabresib to SOC did not improve PFS in patients with ndGBM. Dose reductions and interruptions due to TRAEs were more frequent in the experimental arm and may have negatively impacted PFS. These findings suggest that novel drugs in ndGBM should carefully consider tolerability to ensure proper delivery of SOC and maximize clinical benefit. Dr. M. Simonelli and Dr. M. Vieito have contributed equally to this study.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04324840.
